story: Speech AI barely hears Central Alaskan Yup'ik, as AFN delegates take up resolution 26-20 on permanent federal language funding
stories_surviving: Speech AI and Central Alaskan Yup'ik, pinned to AFN's vote on resolution 26-20
Golden Valley Electric's Energy Emergency Alerts

claims.claim: A Brandeis University survey found no spoken language identification system on HuggingFace that covers Central Alaskan Yup'ik except the largest variant of Meta's MMS-LID family.
claims.verbatim: No system on HuggingFace covers Central Alaskan Yup'ik except the largest variant of Meta's MMS-LID family
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: A Brandeis team that surveyed public models found only one, Meta's largest MMS-LID model, that lists Yup'ik at all.
claims.notes: Read from local extraction out/2026-10-20/yupik_paper.txt (abstract). This is the authors' survey of HuggingFace at time of writing, so attribute it. Paper dated July 3rd, outside the news window, use as background to the AFN peg. Curly apostrophe in Meta's normalized.

claims.claim: Whisper, VoxLingua107-based models and ESPnet OWSM include Hawaiian and Maori but neither Samoan nor any Yupik variety.
claims.verbatim: include Hawaiian and Maori but neither Samoan nor any Yupik variety
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 1 text, consistent with Table 1 checkmarks (haw and mi ticked, smo, esu, ess blank for these three).

claims.claim: The paper's Table 1 lists Whisper large-v3 as covering 99 languages.
claims.verbatim: Whisper large-v3 99
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 1 row.

claims.claim: The paper's Table 1 lists VoxLingua107 as covering 107 languages.
claims.verbatim: VoxLingua107 107
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 1 row. The PDF extraction splits the name as 'V oxLingua107' (kerning noise).

claims.claim: The paper's Table 1 lists ESPnet OWSM v4 as covering about 150 languages.
claims.verbatim: ESPnet OWSM v4∼150
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: roughly 150 languages
claims.notes: Table 1 gives an approximate figure (tilde), so print it as approximate.

claims.claim: Meta's MMS-LID family covers Yup'ik only at its largest variant, which has 4,017 labels.
claims.verbatim: covers Yup'ik only at the largest 4017-label variant
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Corroborated by C39 (Meta's MMS paper, 4,017 languages) and C40 (HuggingFace model card lists esu and ess).

claims.claim: At 4,017 labels the per-class prior is about 2.5 x 10^-4, which the authors say makes zero-shot results on under-represented languages poor.
claims.verbatim: At 4017 labels, the per-class prior is approximately 2.5×10 −4, and zero-shot performance on under-represented languages is accordingly poor.
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Sanity check passes, 1 divided by 4,017 is 0.000249. A friendlier deck phrasing is 'about 1 in 4,000'. Superscript minus is extraction noise in the verbatim.

claims.claim: Zero-shot on the Yup'ik test clips, mms-lid-4017 reached a precision of 0.85 on the Yup'ik label.
claims.verbatim: It achieves high precision (0.85) but low recall (0.41)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 5 Finding 2, matches Table 5 row 'target .85 .41 .55'.

claims.claim: Zero-shot on the Yup'ik test clips, mms-lid-4017 reached a recall of 0.41 on the Yup'ik label.
claims.verbatim: It achieves high precision (0.85) but low recall (0.41)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Plain-English reading is that the model caught about 4 in 10 Yup'ik clips. Cross-check note, Table 6 gives 110 correct esu predictions and Table 3 gives 283 gold esu segments, which is 0.39 rather than 0.41, so the evaluated subset likely differs slightly from Table 3. Print the paper's 0.41 and do not recompute it from the tables.

claims.claim: Zero-shot on the Yup'ik test clips, mms-lid-4017 reached an F1 score of 0.55 on the Yup'ik label.
claims.verbatim: XLS-R-300M lifts esu recall from 0.41 to 0.85 (F1 0.55→0.82)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Also in Table 5 (mms-lid-4017, Yup'ik videos, target, F1 .55).

claims.claim: For gold Yup'ik clips, the most frequent label mms-lid-4017 predicted was ess, Central Siberian Yupik, with 111 clips.
claims.verbatim: esu ess111
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 6 row (gold esu, predicted ess, count 111). It is listed first, one ahead of the correct label (C12). The ess expansion is in the paper's Table 1 caption and Section 5, and on the ISO 639-3 page (C15).

claims.claim: For gold Yup'ik clips, mms-lid-4017 predicted the correct label esu for 110 clips.
claims.verbatim: esu esu110
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 6. 111 versus 110 is a fair 'neck and neck' framing.

claims.claim: For gold Yup'ik clips, mms-lid-4017 predicted esk, Northwest Alaska Inupiatun, for 16 clips.
claims.verbatim: esu esk16
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 6. The paper itself expands esk as Northwest Alaska Inupiatun in Section 5, see C16.

claims.claim: For gold Yup'ik clips, mms-lid-4017 predicted esi, North Alaskan Inupiatun, for 7 clips.
claims.verbatim: esu esi7
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 6. The paper does not expand esi anywhere. The name North Alaskan Inupiatun comes only from the ISO 639-3 registry (C17).

claims.claim: ISO 639-3 code ess denotes Central Siberian Yupik, a living individual language.
claims.verbatim: Central Siberian Yupik
claims.source_outlet: SIL International, ISO 639-3 Registration Authority
claims.notes: The page shows reference name, Scope Individual and Type Living. The paper's Table 1 caption says the same ('Central Siberian Yupik ess'). The page has no publication date, so date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: ISO 639-3 code esk denotes Northwest Alaska Inupiatun, part of the Inupiaq macrolanguage.
claims.verbatim: Northwest Alaska Inupiatun
claims.source_outlet: SIL International, ISO 639-3 Registration Authority
claims.notes: Two sources agree. The paper (Section 5) says 'Northwest Alaska Inupiatun ( esk)'. The registry page has no date, so date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: ISO 639-3 code esi denotes North Alaskan Inupiatun, part of the Inupiaq macrolanguage.
claims.verbatim: North Alaskan Inupiatun
claims.source_outlet: SIL International, ISO 639-3 Registration Authority
claims.notes: The paper does not name esi, so this expansion rests on the registry only, which is the authoritative source for the code.

claims.claim: The study's Yup'ik audio comes from KYUK, a public broadcaster in western Alaska that has produced Yup'ik television news and programming since the 1970s.
claims.verbatim: KYUK, a public broadcasting station in western Alaska that has produced Yup'ik television news and programming since the 1970s
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 4.1. Corroborated by KYUK's own history page (C43, television began 1972).

claims.claim: The researchers took their audio from the American Archive of Public Broadcasting Online Reading Room, a collaboration between GBH and the Library of Congress.
claims.verbatim: We take data from the AAPB Online Reading Room
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: The GBH and Library of Congress detail is in the Acknowledgments ('a collaboration between GBH and the U.S. Library of Congress'). The authors say they do not redistribute the source audio.

claims.claim: The annotated Yup'ik set covers 9 videos.
claims.verbatim: Videos annotated 9 6
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 3, Yup'ik column first (9), Samoan second (6). The Limitations section repeats '9 Yup'ik and 6 Samoan videos'.

claims.claim: The annotated Yup'ik set runs 5.1 hours.
claims.verbatim: Total duration 5.1 h 5.1 h
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 3. Both languages happen to be 5.1 h.

claims.claim: The annotated Yup'ik set contains 589 segments.
claims.verbatim: Total segments 589 1,189
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 3. Sanity check passes, 283 esu plus 238 eng plus 53 mixed plus 15 other is 589.

claims.claim: 283 of the Yup'ik set's segments are labeled as Yup'ik speech, esu.
claims.verbatim: labeledesu/smo283 685
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Table 3, primary annotator's labels. Extraction runs the words together ('labeled esu/smo 283 685').

claims.claim: A small classifier head trained on a frozen Whisper-medium encoder raised Yup'ik recall to 0.92.
claims.verbatim: Whisper-medium lifts it further to 0.92 (F1 0.94)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: In a pilot, a small add-on trained on about 1,600 labeled clips caught 92 percent of Yup'ik clips.
claims.notes: Table 7 shows esu P .96 R .92 F1 .94. This is not an apples-to-apples comparison with C09. The authors note the head emits only four labels, so the esu and ess confusion is 'absent here by construction'. Pair it with the pilot caveat (C30).

claims.claim: With the frozen Whisper-medium encoder the Yup'ik F1 score reached 0.94.
claims.verbatim: Whisper-medium lifts it further to 0.92 (F1 0.94)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: pilot-scale result
claims.notes: Table 7. Same caveats as C24.

claims.claim: The same classifier head on a frozen XLS-R-300M encoder raised Yup'ik recall to 0.85.
claims.verbatim: XLS-R-300M lifts esu recall from 0.41 to 0.85 (F1 0.55→0.82)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: pilot-scale result
claims.notes: Table 7 shows esu P .79 R .85 F1 .82.

claims.claim: With the frozen XLS-R-300M encoder the Yup'ik F1 score reached 0.82.
claims.verbatim: XLS-R-300M lifts esu recall from 0.41 to 0.85 (F1 0.55→0.82)
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: pilot-scale result
claims.notes: Table 7.

claims.claim: The prototype is a two-layer MLP trained on fixed features from a frozen pretrained speech encoder.
claims.verbatim: train a two-layer MLP (1024→256→4, with ReLU and dropout) on those fixed features
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 6. Evaluated with 15-fold leave-one-video-out cross-validation.

claims.claim: The prototype was trained on about 1,600 labeled clips across both Yup'ik and Samoan, in four coarse classes.
claims.verbatim: about 1.6k labeled clips and four coarse classes
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: about 1,600 labeled clips in Yup'ik, Samoan and English combined
claims.notes: IMPORTANT, this is the combined two-language set across 15 videos, not 1,600 Yup'ik clips. The Yup'ik set alone is 589 segments (C22). Sanity check, 589 plus 1,189 minus 89 'other' gives 1,689, consistent with the paper's 'about 1.6k'. The pilot caveat says 'about 1.6k labeled segments'.

claims.claim: The authors say their prototype results should be treated as pilot-scale evidence.
claims.verbatim: should be treated as pilot-scale evidence rather than settled levels
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 6 'Pilot-scale caveat'. Any slide quoting C24 to C27 should carry this.

claims.claim: The authors' next step is to move primary annotation to trained native-speaker annotators.
claims.verbatim: transitioning primary annotation to trained native-speaker annotators, who will expand the dataset over the coming months
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: The authors plan to hand annotation to trained native speakers.
claims.notes: Section 7.2. Forward-looking, so phrase it as a plan.

claims.claim: Since the paper's first submission, community language fellows have begun annotating Yup'ik and Samoan broadcast material.
claims.verbatim: a larger-scale annotation effort has begun with community language fellows working directly on Yup'ik and Samoan broadcast materials
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: according to the paper
claims.notes: Section 7.2. The paper gives no count of fellows and no names.

claims.claim: The current annotated set was labeled by in-house researchers rather than native speakers.
claims.verbatim: was produced by in-house researcher annotators rather than native speakers
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Limitations section. Dual annotation gave Cohen's kappa 0.67, and Yup'ik labels agreed 84 percent (112 of 133). Disclose this alongside any accuracy figure.

claims.claim: The paper describes Yup'ik as having a four-vowel system with contrastive vowel length.
claims.verbatim: a four-vowel system with contrastive vowel length
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 2, citing Woodbury 1987 and Jacobson 1995. Table 2 shows 'Vowel inventory 4'.

claims.claim: The paper's Table 2 puts the Yup'ik consonant inventory at about 25.
claims.verbatim: Consonant inventory∼25∼13∼24
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.suggested_phrasing: about 25 consonants
claims.notes: Approximate figure (tilde). Columns are Yup'ik about 25, Samoan about 13, English about 24.

claims.claim: The paper says Yup'ik has acoustically distinctive sounds rare across languages, including velar and uvular consonants and voiceless nasals.
claims.value: velar and uvular consonants, voiceless nasals
claims.verbatim: including velar and uvular consonants as well as voiceless nasals
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Section 2 ('acoustically salient but cross-linguistically rare features'). Table 2 ticks both for Yup'ik only.

claims.claim: The paper by Yangyang Chen, Kyeongmin Rim and James Pustejovsky of Brandeis University appeared in the AmericasNLP 2026 workshop proceedings on July 3rd.
claims.verbatim: July 3, 2026 ©2026 Association for Computational Linguistics
claims.source_outlet: ACL Anthology
claims.notes: The verbatim is the PDF header. The landing page confirms the title, the authors, pages 203 to 211, and the Sixth Workshop on NLP for Indigenous Languages of the Americas, San Diego, July 2026. Background, since it is outside the news window.

claims.claim: The research was supported in part by the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation.
claims.verbatim: This research was supported in part by Andrew W. Mellon Foundation.
claims.source_outlet: Chen, Rim and Pustejovsky (Brandeis University), AmericasNLP 2026 proceedings, ACL Anthology
claims.notes: Acknowledgments.

claims.claim: Meta's Massively Multilingual Speech paper describes a language identification model for 4,017 languages.
claims.verbatim: a language identification model for 4,017 languages
claims.source_outlet: Pratap et al. (Meta AI), arXiv
claims.notes: Abstract of 'Scaling speech technology to 1,000+ languages', submitted May 22nd, 2023. Background.

claims.claim: Meta's mms-lid-4017 model card on HuggingFace says the model supports 4017 languages.
claims.verbatim: This model supports 4017 languages.
claims.source_outlet: Meta (facebook) on HuggingFace
claims.notes: The model card's supported-language list includes both esu and ess, which corroborates the paper's Table 1. The page is undated, so date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: KYUK's licensee operates public radio and television stations in Bethel, Alaska.
claims.verbatim: operating public radio and television stations located in Bethel, Alaska
claims.source_outlet: KYUK (Bethel Broadcasting, Inc.)
claims.notes: The page describes 'Bethel Broadcasting, Inc. is a Native American initiated public broadcasting joint licensee'. The AAPB profile also lists 'KYUK Bethel, Alaska'. The page is undated, so date_of_source is the fetch date.

claims.claim: KYUK radio has been on the air since 1971.
claims.verbatim: KYUK AM has been on the air since 1971.
claims.source_outlet: KYUK (Bethel Broadcasting, Inc.)
claims.notes: Corroborated by the AAPB profile ('KYUK first began broadcasting radio to the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta in 1971').

claims.claim: KYUK television began broadcasting in 1972.
claims.verbatim: KYUK television began broadcasting in 1972.
claims.source_outlet: KYUK (Bethel Broadcasting, Inc.)
claims.notes: The same sentence appears on the AAPB KYUK profile. Consistent with the paper's 'since the 1970s'.

claims.claim: KYUK broadcasts about one hour a day of local news in Yup'ik.
claims.verbatim: KYUK broadcasts approximately one hour a day of local news in the Yup'ik language.
claims.source_outlet: KYUK (Bethel Broadcasting, Inc.)
claims.suggested_phrasing: about an hour a day, according to KYUK
claims.notes: The identical sentence is on the AAPB profile. The page is undated, so treat the figure as current per KYUK. Curly apostrophe normalized. Do NOT use the Yup'ik public-affairs hours, because KYUK's page says 5.5 hours a week while AAPB says 1.5 hours five days a week (see killed).

claims.claim: KYUK describes itself as a bilingual station broadcasting in English and Yugtun.
claims.verbatim: As a result, KYUK is a bilingual station, broadcasting in both English and Yugtun.
claims.source_outlet: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, KYUK participating-organization profile
claims.notes: The profile text is written in KYUK's voice ('we are in the process'), so it is treated as the station's own statement. The page is undated.

claims.claim: KYUK radio serves about 22,000 mostly Yup'ik and Cup'ik residents of the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta.
claims.verbatim: KYUK radio serves a population of approximately 22,000 predominantly Yup'ik/Cup'ik residents in the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta
claims.source_outlet: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, KYUK participating-organization profile
claims.suggested_phrasing: about 22,000 people, by KYUK's estimate
claims.notes: Undated self-description, single source. The sentence continues past the quoted portion.

claims.claim: KYUK says it is digitizing more than 2,000 videos to make them public.
claims.verbatim: With help from our funders, we are in the process of digitizing over 2,000 videos and making them available to the public.
claims.source_outlet: American Archive of Public Broadcasting, KYUK participating-organization profile
claims.suggested_phrasing: KYUK has said it is digitizing more than 2,000 videos
claims.notes: Undated statement, so progress is unknown. This is NOT a count of KYUK items held by AAPB. No such count could be retrieved (see killed).

claims.claim: Yup'ik has the largest body of speakers of any Alaska Native language, according to the Alaska Native Languages site.
claims.verbatim: Yup'ik has the largest body of speakers of any Native language in Alaska, with 10,400 native speakers.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Native Languages (alaskanativelanguages.org), maps credited to the Alaska Native Language Center
claims.suggested_phrasing: the most widely spoken Alaska Native language
claims.notes: The ranking is widely repeated, and Wikipedia cites Census Bureau data placing Yup'ik second only to Navajo nationally, but that primary source was not fetched. The page footer is (c) 2024 with no study date. ANLC pages on uaf.edu returned 503.

claims.claim: The Alaska Native Languages site puts the number of native Yup'ik speakers at 10,400.
claims.verbatim: Yup'ik has the largest body of speakers of any Native language in Alaska, with 10,400 native speakers.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Native Languages (alaskanativelanguages.org)
claims.suggested_phrasing: roughly 10,000 native speakers, by one undated estimate
claims.notes: DISPUTED AND UNDATED. The page gives no year or study. Other figures in circulation (Census ACS 2009 to 2013 at 19,750, and 'more than 14,000') were seen only on Wikipedia and not verified at a primary source. Prefer leaving the number out, or attribute it and say it is an estimate.

claims.claim: Central Alaskan Yup'ik is spoken in Southwest Alaska from Bristol Bay to Norton Sound.
claims.verbatim: Central Alaskan Yup'ik is spoken in Southwest Alaska from the Bristol Bay to Norton Sound.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Native Languages (alaskanativelanguages.org)
claims.notes: Consistent with the paper's 'spoken in western Alaska' (Section 2).

claims.claim: St. Lawrence Island Yupik is spoken by about 1,000 people on St. Lawrence Island, according to the Alaska Native Languages site.
claims.verbatim: is spoken by about 1,000 people on St. Lawrence Island
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Native Languages (alaskanativelanguages.org)
claims.suggested_phrasing: spoken on St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea
claims.notes: Undated count. The location is solid (Glottolog corroborates, C53), but the number is soft. Wikipedia, citing ANLPAC, gives 400 to 750 US speakers, which conflicts. Prefer the location without the number.

claims.claim: The same Yupik language is also spoken in eastern Russia.
claims.verbatim: it is spoken by 300 Yupik people in Eastern Russia.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Native Languages (alaskanativelanguages.org)
claims.suggested_phrasing: and across the Bering Strait in Russia
claims.notes: Location corroborated by Glottolog (countries Russian Federation and United States, C53). The '300' figure is undated, and Wikipedia cites a 2021 Russian census figure of 172, so do not print the count.

claims.claim: Glottolog lists St. Lawrence Island Yupik as an alternative name for Central Siberian Yupik and records it in Russia and the United States.
claims.verbatim: St. Lawrence Island Yupik
claims.source_outlet: Glottolog (Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology)
claims.notes: The languoid 'Central Siberian Yupik' (cent2128) has countries 'Russian Federation [RU]' and 'United States [US]', and the alternative names include 'St. Lawrence Island Yupik'. This links the model's confusion label ess to the language spoken on St. Lawrence Island, so a deck can say the model mistook Yup'ik for its neighbor across the Bering Sea.

claims.claim: AFN draft resolution 26-20 is titled a resolution supporting national Indigenous language revitalization, Tribal self-governance and permanent federal funding.
claims.verbatim: A RESOLUTION SUPPORTING NATIONAL INDIGENOUS LANGUAGE REVITALIZATION, TRIBAL SELF-GOVERNANCE, AND PERMANENT FEDERAL FUNDING
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: Read from local extraction out/2026-10-20/afn_resolutions.txt, packet pages 51 to 53, marked CONVENTION DRAFT. It is resolution 20 in the Education section of the table of contents.

claims.claim: Resolution 26-20 calls on Congress and the Administration to establish permanent, non-competitive federal funding for all eligible Tribal Nations to revitalize their languages.
claims.verbatim: calls upon Congress and the Administration to establish permanent, non-competitive federal funding for all eligible Tribal Nations to revitalize their languages
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.suggested_phrasing: The draft resolution, if adopted, would call on Congress...
claims.notes: It is a draft until delegates vote. The source operative clause reads 'NOW THEREFORE BE IT that' with 'RESOLVED' missing (typo in the source). It also seeks non-discretionary advance appropriations 'without statutory caps or pilot limits'.

claims.claim: Resolution 26-20 lists technology among the uses Tribes could fund, alongside immersion schools, master-apprentice programs, curriculum, archives and community-based transmission.
claims.verbatim: immersion schools, master-apprentice programs, curriculum development, technology, archives, and community-based transmission
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: The clause says funding 'shall be administered under self-governance principles, allowing Tribes to design, manage, and evaluate their own language revitalization strategies'.

claims.claim: Resolution 26-20 states that competitive, short-term grant funding has proven inadequate and inconsistent with Tribal self-determination.
claims.verbatim: Competitive, discretionary, short-term grant funding has proven inadequate, inefficient, and inconsistent with Tribal self-determination
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.suggested_phrasing: the resolution argues
claims.notes: A WHEREAS clause, so attribute it as the resolution's position.

claims.claim: The full text of resolution 26-20 names technology as a fundable use but never mentions artificial intelligence.
claims.verbatim: curriculum development, technology, archives, and community-based transmission
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: Checked by reading the whole of 26-20 (packet pages 51 to 53). An absence can't be proved by quote, so the verbatim shows the only technology reference. The bridge from 26-20 to speech AI is the deck's own framing, not AFN's, and the copy must make that clear.

claims.claim: Resolution 26-20 was submitted by the Metlakatla Indian Community and the Ketchikan Indian Community.
claims.verbatim: SUBMITTED BY: METLAKATLA INDIAN COMMUNITY & KETCHIKAN INDIAN COMMUNITY
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives

claims.claim: AFN's resolutions committee recommended do pass on resolution 26-20.
claims.verbatim: COMMITTEE ACTION: DO PASS
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: Appears directly under the 26-20 submitter line. The same string recurs on other resolutions, so cite the 26-20 page (packet page 52).

claims.claim: AFN's board recommended do pass on resolution 26-20.
claims.verbatim: BOARD ACTION: DO PASS
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: Packet page 52.

claims.claim: In the September 27th draft packet the convention action line for resolution 26-20 is blank, so delegates had not yet voted.
claims.verbatim: CONVENTION ACTION:
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.suggested_phrasing: goes to a delegate vote on Saturday
claims.notes: Packet page 53, carried over from page 52. The outcome is unknown as of the run date, so do not imply passage.

claims.claim: AFN's resolutions state that its membership includes 192 federally recognized tribes.
claims.verbatim: its membership includes 192 federally recognized tribes, 152 village corporations, 11 regional corporations and 11 regional nonprofit and tribal consortiums
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: Preamble of 26-01, repeated in every resolution read including 26-20. Not to be confused with 26-45's 'Alaska is home to 229 federally recognized tribes', which counts all Alaska tribes, not AFN members.

claims.claim: AFN's resolutions state that its membership includes 152 village corporations.
claims.verbatim: its membership includes 192 federally recognized tribes, 152 village corporations, 11 regional corporations and 11 regional nonprofit and tribal consortiums
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: 26-01 preamble.

claims.claim: AFN's resolutions state that its membership includes 11 regional corporations.
claims.verbatim: its membership includes 192 federally recognized tribes, 152 village corporations, 11 regional corporations and 11 regional nonprofit and tribal consortiums

claims.claim: AFN's 2026 draft resolution packet contains 48 resolutions.
claims.verbatim: 48 VOTE NO ON 2 TO PROTECT ALASKA'S OPEN PRIMARY, RANKED CHOICE VOTING, AND DARK MONEY DISCLOSURE ELECTION SYSTEM
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: The table of contents runs from 1 to 48 with no gaps, and the last resolution in the body is 26-48. The verbatim has its curly apostrophe normalized.

claims.claim: None of the 48 resolution titles in AFN's 2026 draft packet names artificial intelligence, AI or data centers.
claims.verbatim: 46 RESOLUTION FOR A NEW COMPREHENSIVE DATABASE FOR UNKNOWN ALASKA NATIVE CHILDREN BURIED IN A PUYALLUP CEMETERY.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.suggested_phrasing: None of the 48 draft resolution titles mention AI.
claims.notes: SCOPE, the check covers all 48 titles in the table of contents (packet pages 1 to 3). The full body text of all 48 was NOT checked, so claim titles only. The only 'data' term in any title is 26-46's 'database', quoted here as the nearest miss. Resolution 26-20's body was read in full and also has no AI mention (C58).

claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: The fields it lists include 'Alaska Native Languages'. Committee and board action are both DO PASS.

claims.claim: Resolution 26-47 urges Congress to appropriate 14.9 million dollars a year to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to sustain 36 Native radio stations and one Tribally licensed television station.
claims.verbatim: urges Congress to appropriate annual funding total $14.9 million to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to sustain the thirty-six Native radio stations, one Tribally licensed television station
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.suggested_phrasing: a draft resolution urges
claims.notes: Relevant because KYUK is the paper's Yup'ik audio source. The deck must NOT imply that KYUK is among the 36 Native-controlled stations, because the resolution names no stations. Its internal figures differ ($9.7 million in FY2025 grants, $13.9 million total loss, $14.9 million ask), so quote only the ask. The final clause also urges the state to restore funding for '27 Alaska public media stations'.

claims.source_outlet: Alaska Federation of Natives
claims.notes: 'SUBMITTTED' with three Ts is in the source. Committee and board action are both DO PASS.
